supplement.where: No separate supplement or online appendix is referenced in the complete PDF. The Data Availability Statement says 'Data are contained within the article' (p. 28). Table 12 (p. 20) is an in-article supplementary analysis; the supplementary course on p. 11 is instruction supplied to the control group.

paper_design_summary: 120 second-year visual communication design undergraduates were individually randomized to separately taught classes of 60 for a six-week illustration course: GenAI embedded throughout design thinking versus traditional instruction with sporadic GenAI use (pp. 9-11). Six experts evaluated 24 final group projects on creativity, applicability, technicality, expressiveness, and completeness; the overall score averaged the five dimensions (pp. 11-12, 20-22). The study analyzed 120 students for questionnaire/SEM results and 24 projects for output comparisons; project membership and the number of distinct students represented by the rated projects are not reported (pp. 15, 20-21).

studies.label: Six-week illustration course experiment (GenAI-integrated vs traditional instruction)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Instructional model for a six-week Illustration Design course: GenAI integrated throughout design thinking versus traditional teaching with sporadic GenAI. Students were individually allocated by computer randomization of student IDs, then taught in separate classes by the same team of lecturers; assignments remained fixed (p. 9, Section 3.4.1; p. 10, Section 3.4.3).
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned at the individual level into an experimental group and a control group, with 60 students in each group, and the two groups were taught in separate classes.

arms.name: Experimental (Integrated Teaching Model)
arms.description: GenAI embedded in the five design-thinking stages (Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test), with explicit tool-intervention points, workshops, group collaboration, and iterative cycles. Evaluation combined outcomes and processes, expert evaluation, peer and lecturer co-assessment, and motivational analysis (p. 10, Section 3.4.3; p. 11, Table 2).

arms.name: Control (Traditional Teaching Model)
arms.description: Traditional lecturer-led instruction and case analysis, primarily independent assignments, and mainly final-outcome evaluation. GenAI was used sporadically for sketch generation, style reference, or material preparation; manual drawing and conventional digital software remained dominant (p. 10, Section 3.4.3; p. 11, Table 2).

participants.exclusions: No exclusions or attrition are reported. Random assignment was 60 students per arm (p. 9, Section 3.4.1); the questionnaire analysis reports 60 per arm (p. 15, Table 7), and the SEM analysis explicitly reports 120 students (p. 20, Section 4.6). The output analysis uses 24 group projects, listed as W01–W12/Exp and W13–W24/Ctrl (p. 21, Table 13). Team formation, team sizes, and the number of distinct students contributing to these projects are not stated; 24 projects must not be described as 24 people or assumed to be 24 distinct teams.
participants.who: Second-year undergraduates majoring in Visual Communication Design, same major and cohort, enrolled in the Illustration Design course in one semester at 'College X', volunteers
participants.quote: whereas the SEM analysis was performed at the student level (n = 120), focusing on patterns observed in the learning process.
participants.locator: p. 20, Section 4.6 (students analyzed); p. 15, Table 7 (60 analyzed per arm); p. 9, Sections 3.4–3.4.1 (recruitment and assignment)

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT, Midjourney, Stable Diffusion, Runway, and unspecified AIGC/emotion-analysis tools (p. 7, Figure 2); intervention model versions not stated.
ai_tool.how_used: Figure 2 (p. 7) names ChatGPT and Midjourney for user profiles and scene contexts in week 1; ChatGPT and Stable Diffusion for keyword clustering and question statements in week 2; Midjourney and Stable Diffusion for creative divergence and visual generation in week 3; AIGC-assisted illustration generation, layout, and visual optimization in week 4; and Runway and AI for emotion analysis, feedback analysis, and design optimization in week 5. Week 6 covers project presentation, expert evaluation, self/peer assessment, and reflection. The control arm used GenAI sporadically during sketching or material preparation (p. 10, Section 3.4.3). DALL·E and ChatGPT-4 appear as baseline-survey examples (p. 9), not as confirmed intervention models.

task.description: Final group illustration-design projects from the Illustration Design course, presented to experts as final images, brief design statements, and key process summaries (p. 12, Section 3.5.1).
task.duration: Six-week course (p. 9, Section 3.4.1); matched teaching weeks, in-class hours, assignment windows, and final submission deadline (p. 12, Section 3.5.1).

outcomes.name: Overall expert evaluation score of final project (mean of five dimensions)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Six experts with teaching and industry experience in illustration and visual communication rated anonymized final group projects in randomized order in an on-site panel session (pp. 11–12, Section 3.5.1). The overall project score is the mean of five dimensions on a 100-point scale: creativity, applicability, technicality, expressiveness, and completeness (p. 12, Table 3). The composite is coded other because it combines novelty, applied quality, craftsmanship, esthetic communication, and coherence. Reported reliability: ICC(2,k) = 0.924, 95% CI [0.847, 0.947]; ICC(2,1) = 0.670 (p. 22, Table 14). The paper describes independent scoring followed by discussion to consensus but does not identify whether the table and ICC use initial or consensus scores (p. 20, Section 4.6).

contrasts.reported: Experimental M = 86.58, SD = 1.84; control M = 79.94, SD = 2.98; independent-sample project-level t-test, n = 24 projects, t(22) = 6.57, p < 0.001; Cohen’s d = 2.68. Table 13 lists W01–W12/Exp and W13–W24/Ctrl, corresponding to 12 projects per arm. These are project-level statistics, not student-level scores.
contrasts.locator: p. 20, Section 4.6; p. 21, Table 13; p. 22, Figure 6, Final grade panel

eligibility.reason: All three criteria are met in S1. Individual students were allocated by computer randomization to different GenAI instructional configurations (p. 9, Section 3.4.1; pp. 10-11, Section 3.4.3 and Table 2). The study analyzed 120 students, with 60 per arm in the questionnaire analysis (p. 15, Table 7; p. 20, Section 4.6), meeting the current form-spec threshold of at least 50 analyzed people across the study. Experts scored novelty and output quality on students’ final group projects produced with GenAI available (pp. 11-12, Section 3.5.1 and Table 3; p. 21, Table 13). Expressiveness and Completeness are coded usefulness because they rate qualities of individual outputs. The creativity comparison analyzes 24 projects; the number of distinct contributing students and team membership are not reported, so 120 must not be treated as the number of independent creative scores. Both arms use GenAI, and the instructional contrast also changes pedagogy and uses separate classes; the comparison is ai_design.

one_line_finding: Across 24 group projects, instruction integrating GenAI throughout design thinking had higher overall expert scores than traditional instruction with sporadic GenAI (86.58 [SD 1.84] vs 79.94 [SD 2.98]; t(22) = 6.57, p < 0.001, d = 2.68; p. 20, Section 4.6).
open_questions: How many distinct students contributed to the rated projects, and how were teams formed? The article reports 120 students for SEM and 24 group projects for output analysis but supplies no membership mapping (pp. 12, 20–21).

Do Table 13 and the ICC calculations use the experts' initial independent scores or scores after discussion to consensus? Both procedures are described, without identifying the dataset used for each statistic (pp. 20–22).

What does each Figure 6 scatter point represent? The p. 21 text calls them individual expert ratings, while visual inspection is compatible with the project means in Table 13; no plot data or aggregation procedure is supplied (pp. 21–22).
notes: The complete markdown was read from beginning to end, including references; the 31-page PDF has no appendix. Figure 2 was inspected directly because the conversion and PDF text omit its rasterized labels. Every retained numerical statistic was checked against the PDF; project scores were transcribed from Table 13 without computing arm summaries or effect sizes. The unit is output (a group project), correcting both raw forms' team label: the paper explicitly analyzes projects and does not identify distinct teams. n_analyzed = 120 is the reported student-level questionnaire/SEM sample, not a confirmed person count for the rated projects. The six retained outcomes are the composite and its five dimensions, not six independent studies. Dimension contrasts retain figure_only because the form has no category for numeric project-level data without an arm-level estimate; exact project values are nevertheless preserved. Self-reported cognitive-load, ARCS, and perceived teaching-alignment measures are excluded from output outcomes; they were collected at course end on a five-point Likert scale (p. 13, Section 3.5.2 and Table 4). The baseline design task is a pretest, with control 74.6 ± 6.8 and experimental 75.4 ± 7.1, assessed by two course instructors (p. 10, Table 1 and Section 3.4.2); it is not an after_ai outcome. Interviews with two lecturers and 10 experimental-group students are qualitative (p. 13, Section 3.5.3). The control group received the integrated course after the experiment (p. 11, Section 3.4.4). IRB approval was 22 August 2025 (p. 28). No after_ai or across_people output outcome is reported. The ai_design and novelty codes are settled using the control's explicit AI use and the Creativity rubric's explicit novelty focus; these are not unresolved coding choices. Reconciliation counts substantive additional methodological details and numerical evidence, but not equivalent labels, wording, compatible locators, or repetitions of the same issue. The unresolved-difference count refers to A–B differences; shared reporting gaps remain in open_questions. Final review confirmed both outcome challenges against PDF p. 12, Table 3: Expressiveness and Completeness are coded usefulness under the codebook’s output-quality definition. The reconciliation object is retained unchanged as the prior review record; the operative construct codes are in studies and final. The three remaining reporting gaps, including the duplicate unresolved reconciliation item, are classified in final.open_items.

differences.a: Questionnaire outcomes (cognitive load IL/EL/GL, ARCS motivation AT/RE/CF/SA, ITA; Table 7, p. 15; PLS-SEM, MICOM, MGA in Tables 8-12) are self-reported and are not listed as outcomes. The control group received the integrated course content after the experiment (p. 11). IRB: Hanyang University, approved 22 August 2025 (p. 28). differences.b: Questionnaire outcomes (intrinsic, extraneous, germane load; attention, relevance, confidence, satisfaction; integrated teaching alignment) are self-reports on a five-point Likert scale collected at the end of the course (Table 4, p. 13; Table 7, p. 15; PLS-SEM and MGA in Tables 8-12) and are not listed as outcomes. Baseline design-task score (Table 1, p. 10: control 74.6 +/- 6.8, experimental 75.4 +/- 7.1, rated by two course instructors) is a pretest, not an outcome. Structured interviews with 2 lecturers and 10 experimental-group students (p. 13) are qualitative. IRB approval: Hanyang University, 22 August 2025 (p. 28). Control group received the integrated course content after the experiment (p. 11).
differences.resolved: The complete markdown was read from beginning to end, including references; the 31-page PDF has no appendix. Figure 2 was inspected directly because the conversion and PDF text omit its rasterized labels. Every retained numerical statistic was checked against the PDF; project scores were transcribed from Table 13 without computing arm summaries or effect sizes. The unit is output (a group project), correcting both raw forms' team label: the paper explicitly analyzes projects and does not identify distinct teams. n_analyzed = 120 is the reported student-level questionnaire/SEM sample, not a confirmed person count for the rated projects. The six retained outcomes are the composite and its five dimensions, not six independent studies. Dimension contrasts retain figure_only because the form has no category for numeric project-level data without an arm-level estimate; exact project values are nevertheless preserved. Self-reported cognitive-load, ARCS, and perceived teaching-alignment measures are excluded from output outcomes; they were collected at course end on a five-point Likert scale (p. 13, Section 3.5.2 and Table 4). The baseline design task is a pretest, with control 74.6 ± 6.8 and experimental 75.4 ± 7.1, assessed by two course instructors (p. 10, Table 1 and Section 3.4.2); it is not an after_ai outcome. Interviews with two lecturers and 10 experimental-group students are qualitative (p. 13, Section 3.5.3). The control group received the integrated course after the experiment (p. 11, Section 3.4.4). IRB approval was 22 August 2025 (p. 28). No after_ai or across_people output outcome is reported. The ai_design and novelty codes are settled using the control's explicit AI use and the Creativity rubric's explicit novelty focus; these are not unresolved coding choices. Reconciliation counts substantive additional methodological details and numerical evidence, but not equivalent labels, wording, compatible locators, or repetitions of the same issue. The unresolved-difference count refers to A–B differences; shared reporting gaps remain in open_questions.

open_items.item: open_questions[0]: Distinct student contributors to the rated projects, project membership, team sizes, and team formation remain unreported (pp. 12, 20-21). Author-provided project-to-student membership and team-formation records would settle this. It affects interpretation of the output sample and dependence, but not criterion 2 under the current study-level rule: 120 analyzed students are explicitly reported (p. 20, Section 4.6).

open_questions[1]: Whether Table 13 and the ICC use initial independent ratings or ratings after discussion to consensus remains unresolved (pp. 20-22, Section 4.6 and Tables 13-14). Author-provided initial/final ratings and the scoring and aggregation procedure would settle this. It affects reliability interpretation, but the source already establishes expert scoring of participant-produced outputs, so criterion 3 remains met.

open_questions[2] and the unresolved reconciliation.differences item "open_questions: Figure 6 scatter-point unit": the p. 21 prose calls the points individual expert ratings, while Figure 6 (p. 22) appears compatible with project means. Author-provided plot data or plotting/aggregation code would settle the point unit. This does not affect eligibility: Table 13 and the p. 20 test explicitly analyze projects, and the rated outputs are established independently of Figure 6.
